name: Beth Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a piano trio, teach keyboard at the school and record parts for studios. I’m 27 and have a music master’s, but most mornings still begin with moving a keyboard stand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the best part, and what is the tiring part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when my students hear why a chord works and then make it their own. I dislike chasing invoices, especially when the other players are waiting for their share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau means another handy editing pass, not a different music business. Our trio would still rehearse, and my students would still come to the keyboard room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI every day to sort lesson notes and test a chord sketch, then check it myself. I earn well enough to have nine months of costs saved, so a slow week is manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my three teaching days and the trio’s paid dates this year. On Friday I’d check that the recording clients have paid the agreed fees, then leave my reserve alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work and income in this picture. I am more tired of late clients than worried about a software breakthrough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment is still late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A studio still owes me for a piano part from last month, and I have sent the invoice twice. My rent is covered, but I want the other players paid on time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make more AI music yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still draft with the tool and play the final part myself. A shortcut is useful, but a client pays me for the finished performance.

say: I’d tell the trio **rehearsals** and paid keyboard lessons still need us in the room.
I would welcome a quicker **editing pass** without claiming it changes the whole trade.
think: Daily **AI sketches** help me work, but I check the music before a client hears it.
Nine months of **savings** make one slow recording week manageable.
do: Keep three **teaching days** and the trio’s paid dates this year.
Check unpaid **studio invoices** on Friday before counting them as income.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work and rent in this mild picture.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI daily**, so Plateau is familiar rather than a new threat.
Her strong **reserve** lets her chase overdue fees for fairness to other players, not immediate rent survival.
S0.quote: My rent is covered, but I want the other players paid on time too.

steps.text: Keep three keyboard teaching days and booked trio dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the trio Steady Disruption will make basic arrangements and client replies cheap fast. We should tell players which parts of a job are still paid, rather than hide the loss in a lower fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio could commission fewer piano parts from me, which would cut a real slice of my income. My nine-month reserve buys time, but the other two players do not both have that cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the studio for its expected paid sessions and show the trio the contract terms. If paid sessions drop in the first year, I’d join the musicians’ association pay meeting and test a workshop on human performance, but only after six students pay for the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about my recording income, even with savings. A good year on paper can turn thin if a studio simply stops calling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association meeting change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the association meeting we could agree on a minimum rehearsal fee and ask venues to show it in writing. I would still have to persuade each venue to sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the workshop compete with your current lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One free Saturday would be enough to test a workshop in a rented room. Six paid places would cover the hire and my time; fewer would make me cancel.

say: I’d warn that basic **arrangements** may become cheap and ask clients to name paid human work.
I’d show trio players the **contract terms** before lower fees become normal.
think: Fewer studio **sessions** would cut my income even with nine months of savings.
The other players may lack my **cushion**, which makes hidden fee cuts harder to accept.
do: Ask the **studio** for expected paid sessions and show the trio written terms this month.
Join a **pay meeting** after session cuts; run a Saturday workshop only if six paid places cover room and time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a material cut in studio income despite my reserve.
fieldNote: She makes **collective pay** a practical contract question, consistent with her outlook and concern for the trio.
The **workshop** is conditional on six paid places covering the room and her time.
S1.quote: A good year on paper can turn thin if a studio simply stops calling.

steps.text: Join musicians association pay meeting if studio sessions fall
Run Saturday workshop if sessions drop and six paid places cover room and time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my students AGI by 2028 could take arranging and lesson planning quickly, even though capable robots for hands-on playing follow around 2031. I would not promise the trio that live bookings survive unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose most paid studio composition in two years, but my nine-month reserve and teaching list give me room to move. I worry more about colleagues who cannot wait for a new contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the school now to confirm next year’s paid teaching hours and the trio to list which bookings have deposits. In the first year after 2028, if composition fees stop, I’d add one evening performance class only when the school approves a room and eight students pay; I’d keep the reserve for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, not frozen. My own work could shrink badly, but I have savings and a class I can test without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which task would AGI hit first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short score drafts are already close to what a tool can suggest. A robot able to perform like us comes later, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you hire the trio to teach with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could ask the trio to teach only if eight paid places cover their fees too. I will not call unpaid rehearsal a training opportunity.

say: I’d warn that **arranging** could change in 2028 and capable performance robots follow around 2031.
I would avoid promising **live bookings** that no one has actually paid for.
think: My **studio composition** could fall sharply, though teaching and nine months of savings buy time.
Colleagues without a **reserve** may be forced into poor contracts sooner.
do: Confirm paid **school hours** and trio booking deposits now.
Add one evening **performance class** after 2028 only with school room approval and eight paid students if composition fees stop.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost studio fees, while savings leave me room to act.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking work** from 2031 capable robots for hands-on performance.
The class needs **school approval** and eight paid places; trio teaching would need fees that cover the other players too.
S2.quote: I will not call unpaid rehearsal a training opportunity.

steps.text: Confirm paid school teaching hours and trio booking deposits now
Add evening class if composition fees stop and school room and eight paid students are secured

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives musicians five years to see arranging and recorded work change. Robots capable of playing as people do would follow around 2034, so a live booking still needs its own plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time could let me build a stable teaching programme, but I do not know how much families will pay for it. The studio would probably cut some paid composition by 2031, and I would use the reserve to bridge that gap, not buy a studio on faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the school this spring whether it will fund a yearlong ensemble class and get a written pay rate before offering it. This year I’d test a new ear-training feature on my own recordings and ask students before using their work. In the first year after 2031, I’d continue the class only if ten paid students cover room charges and player wages. I will not spend nine months of savings on a studio full of imaginary pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the studio cutting paid composition, even with savings. Five years lets me ask hard questions before signing a lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ten students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten students would cover the room and two paid players at the current fee. I would recalculate if the school changed the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI to run the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a new ear-training feature on my own recordings first and ask students before using their work. I already use the basic tool, so this feature would be something new to learn.

say: I’d tell players **2031 AGI** leaves time to negotiate paid teaching before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would ask for **written rates** before promising a new ensemble class.
think: A stable **teaching programme** could replace some recording income if families pay.
I will not spend the **reserve** on a studio before demand is proven.
do: Ask the **school** this spring for funding and a written pay rate for ensemble teaching.
Continue the **ensemble class** after 2031 only if ten paid students cover room charges and player wages.
Test the new **ear-training feature** on my own recordings and use student work only with consent.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording income, while savings give me time to test paid teaching.
fieldNote: Her threshold of **ten students** covers the room and two other players, not only her own fee.
She would test a **new AI feature** on her own recordings and seek student consent before using their work.
S3.quote: I will not spend nine months of savings on a studio full of imaginary pupils.

steps.text: Keep school teaching while asking for written ensemble funding and pay
Continue ensemble class after 2031 only if ten paid students cover room and player wages
Test new ear-training feature on own recordings; use student work only with consent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the trio AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to grow the parts of music people still pay for. Thinking work faces AGI in 2036, with capable robots for hands-on performance around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might have a stronger school role and still make records, but I cannot know the audience that far out. I do know I can save and keep my teaching craft fresh without putting other players on free work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my teaching and recording contracts this year, then set aside a fixed share of paid trio fees for the reserve. In the first year after 2036, I’d renew a school class only at a rate that covers players and room costs, and close it if enrollment falls short. If school class funding and recording fees fall, I’d apply to a nearby school with a funded opening while keeping my private pupils until a paid offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years, because my savings and paid work are strong. The long date still makes me check every contract rather than relax forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One quarter of each paid trio fee goes into the reserve after I pay the other players. I would review that share once a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school refuses that rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid private pupils and apply at another nearby school only if it had a funded opening. I would not ask my piano trio to teach without pay when my recording income falls.

say: I’d tell the trio a **decade** lets us grow paid teaching before 2036.
I’d remind players that capable **performance robots** follow thinking AGI around 2039.
think: My current **pay** and reserve make the next few years secure.
I cannot know the **2036 audience**, so I will keep my contracts and teaching current.
do: Keep paid **teaching and recording** contracts this year and reserve a share of trio fees.
Renew a **school class** after 2036 only if its rate covers player wages and room costs.
Keep **private pupils** and apply at a nearby school only if a funded opening exists.
feel: I feel **calm** about near-term work and income, though I still check contracts.
fieldNote: She grounds calm in **paid work**, a strong reserve and many nearby opportunities.
She will close a **class** if enrollment fails rather than ask other players for unpaid labor.
S4.quote: I would not ask my piano trio to teach without pay when my recording income falls.

steps.text: Keep paid teaching and recording contracts this year
Save one quarter of each paid trio fee after paying other players
Renew school class after 2036 only if fees cover player wages and room
Keep paid private pupils and apply at nearby school only if a funded opening exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because studio composition could fall before the trio finds enough paid teaching. Written school hours, rooms for classes and contracts that pay every player would help if that happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask whose time counts when a client says a rehearsal is good exposure. I will keep asking for a fee beside every player’s name, even if my own savings let me walk away.

headlineQuote: I will keep asking for a fee beside every player’s name, even if my own savings let me walk away.
portrait: At **27**, Beth leads a piano trio, teaches keyboard and records parts after earning a music master’s degree.
Her strong **pay**, nine-month reserve and nearby openings give her room to test paid alternatives.
She uses **AI daily** for sketches and notes but checks the music and protects student recordings.
Her progressive **pay concerns** extend to colleagues whose savings cannot carry them through lost studio work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut studio composition before the trio builds enough paid teaching.
whatWouldHelp: Written **school hours**, approved class rooms and contracts paying every player would help.
